editions.title: Anthropic IPO talk builds as Nvidia's Huang faces FBI probe
editions.notification: Anthropic's IPO valuation talk climbs towards $1.5tn while Nvidia shares slide over the Huang probe.
editions.intro:
The biggest story of the period is the twin pressure on Nvidia and the surge of talk around Anthropic. Nvidia shares fell 4.3% on Monday, wiping roughly $190bn off its market value, after a class action accused the company and chief executive Jensen Huang of misleading shareholders over his alleged affair with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive whom US authorities reportedly concluded was a Chinese intelligence asset. Nvidia says it is running an independent investigation, and Donald Trump said the FBI was looking into the matter. Related reports tie Alice Huang to more than $7bn of Nvidia chip sales to China, which could strengthen bipartisan calls to tighten chip export controls.

Anthropic dominated the AI news. The Financial Times reports the company is considering an IPO at up to $1.4tn, with bankers reportedly preparing to lift the target to $1.5tn or more, and Goldman Sachs projects revenue above $600bn by 2030. These are rumours and forecasts, not confirmed plans. The company also released Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, with company-reported gains in coding and research and lower prices, and expanded Claude into a workspace with spreadsheets, whiteboards and data tools.

Elsewhere, AMD detailed its Zen 6 core and its Venice-X and Verano server chips, Alibaba's T-Head filed for a Hong Kong IPO, and the FCC is weighing a ban on Chinese optical transceivers that Microsoft is lobbying against. Regulation was also in focus, with a Paris Call on AI safety signed by ten AI companies but no deadlines or sanctions, and Australia recommending a new AI regulator after an OpenAI-linked breach.

editions.title: Nvidia's Jensen Huang faces board probe over spy reports
editions.notification: Nvidia's CEO is under an independent probe over reported China spy links. Here's what we know so far.
editions.intro:
The dominant story is the crisis at Nvidia. Chief executive Jensen Huang has apologised in an internal memo for an affair, after The New York Times reported that US agencies were examining Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive, over suspected links to China's Ministry of State Security. Nvidia's board has opened an independent investigation, supported by outside counsel, and says it sees no sign that national security or company secrets were compromised. Huang remains CEO. Three Republican House committee chairs have asked for a briefing by 11 November, and Singapore has opened its own probe into Megaspeed. The Chinese government and embassy deny the espionage allegations, and no one has been charged. The suspected operation has not been independently confirmed.

The episode matters well beyond gossip. Nvidia sits at the centre of AI chip supply, and Megaspeed reportedly bought billions of dollars of its chips, while the US Commerce Department has accused the firm of smuggling $2 billion of advanced chips to China. Nvidia shares fell more than 9% in a single session, their steepest daily drop since January 2025, amid a wider chip sell-off that also hit Asian markets. Analysts such as Jeffrey Sonnenfeld put Huang's chances of surviving the probe at roughly even.

Elsewhere, the AI-infrastructure backlash is gathering pace. A new analysis found about 90% of public comments at local government meetings opposed data centres, a Michigan Democrat who campaigned against them won a seat in Congress, and a Texas town-level ban passed with about 77% support. Samsung and SK hynix together hold 329 trillion won in cash, funding record chip spending and shareholder returns.

editions.title: Tech sell-off deepens as Anthropic presses on with IPO and Nvidia faces spy claims
editions.notification: Tech shares slump after the midterms, Tesla winds down Cybertruck, and Anthropic eyes a pre-Thanksgiving IPO.
editions.intro:
Tech markets were rattled this week. The Nasdaq 100 fell 6.4 percent on Thursday, partly recovering on Friday, as rising borrowing costs, heavy AI spending and Democratic midterm wins raised fears of slower data-centre construction. Tesla shares fell 11 percent after Elon Musk said Cybertruck production will wind down around mid-2027, with the Texas plant shifting to the Cybercab robotaxi and Optimus robots. SpaceX dropped 9 percent in the same session, and Musk's fortune reportedly fell by $113bn.

Against that backdrop, Anthropic is reportedly pressing ahead with an IPO before Thanksgiving, seeking $80 to $100 billion at a valuation of $1.25 to $1.75 trillion, below some investors' hopes. OpenAI has reportedly trimmed its funding-round target and raised only about a third of what it sought, though a separate report claims $11bn new funding at a $1.25 trillion valuation. Both are unconfirmed in the material provided.

Nvidia faces its own storm. Three House committee chairs have arranged a closed-door meeting with Jensen Huang over reports that Megaspeed executive Alice Huang may have been recruited by China's intelligence services. Nvidia says its customer contacts are routine, and China has dismissed the claims. Meanwhile, the memory boom continues: DRAM prices are soaring, Samsung's cash pile passed 200 trillion won, and Raspberry Pi and Oppo are feeling the squeeze. Samsung's Taylor, Texas plant may start trial runs in December.

Tech.title: Nvidia faces lawsuit and probe as AI race continues
Tech.notification: Nvidia shares fall $190bn after a lawsuit and FBI probe over Jensen Huang, while AI labs race ahead.
Tech.summary:
The dominant story in tech today is the political and legal fallout around Nvidia and chief executive Jensen Huang. A class action in California accuses Nvidia and Huang of misleading shareholders about his alleged relationship with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive, whom the New York Times reports US authorities consider a Chinese intelligence asset. Nvidia shares closed down 4.3% on Monday, and Nvidia says an independent investigation is under way.

Alongside this, the AI sector keeps moving fast. Anthropic has released Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, and is widely reported to be preparing an IPO at a valuation of up to $1.4tn to $1.5tn, a prospect that has lifted expectations for Amazon and Google, its largest investors. Google DeepMind's Gemini Robotics 2.5 and Gemini 4 Carbon add to the pace of releases, while safety pledges such as the Paris Call show governments and labs seeking common ground.

Chip supply and China remain central. Morgan Stanley has cut its price targets on SK hynix and Samsung on concerns about a 2028 earnings cliff, while Washington debates limits on Chinese optical transceivers and tighter controls on chip flows to China.

highlights.text: Shares fell 4.3% on Monday, wiping about $190bn. Nvidia says it is running an independent investigation, and Trump said the FBI is looking into the matter.

Finance.title: Hot inflation sets up Fed hike as Nvidia scandal weighs
Finance.notification: US inflation ran hotter than expected and Nvidia lost $430bn in two days. Here is what it means for markets.
Finance.summary:
US consumer prices rose 0.4% in October, above the 0.3% forecast, and core inflation rose 0.3%, against 0.2% expected. Markets had already priced in a quarter-point Federal Reserve rate hike in December, and Treasury yields, the dollar and US stocks all reacted. Oil and the US-Iran war remain a central driver, with Brent easing towards $91 on hopes of a peace deal.

Nvidia dominated the week's corporate news. Its shares fell sharply after the company opened an inquiry into chief executive Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, whom US intelligence reportedly considers a Chinese asset. Microsoft overtook it as the second most valuable company, and investors have launched a class action. Anthropic's IPO, with a range of $70 to $78 a share, is due to start trading next week and is being watched as a test of AI appetite.

In the UK, the FTSE 100 closed lower after early gains faded, with miners and oil majors weighing. Poundland's fight to avoid administration and the Vodafone results were the main domestic company stories. In Europe, the focus was on Infineon's AI power-chip outlook and Spain's election campaign, while in Asia the Kospi's sharp sell-off and Japan's security planning were in focus.

World.title: Trump says Iran war is over as Hegseth faces impeachment bid
World.notification: Trump says the Iran war is militarily over, but oil traders and Congress remain on edge.
World.summary:
US politics dominated the day after heavy Republican losses in the midterms. President Trump said the Iran war was militarily "effectively over", with further strikes unlikely and talks showing positive momentum, and oil futures slid on the remarks. Iranian officials have doubted such claims, and European ministers said they could not rule out renewed escalation over the Strait of Hormuz.

Congress was the other focus. A House vote of 211 to 204 sent Republican Thomas Massie's impeachment articles against Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth to committee, effectively halting them for now, though Democrats take control in January and could revive the effort. Markets were also rattled by a hotter-than-expected October inflation report, which strengthened the case for a Federal Reserve rate rise in December and pushed Wall Street lower at the open.

Beyond Washington, the UK saw a new Labour high in one poll under Andy Burnham, while Europe and Asia were dominated by Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi and a Spanish general strike.

Fashion.title: Creative shake-ups and deal talk reshape luxury
Fashion.notification: Capri's next chief executive may be lined up, while Balenciaga gets a new designer from Martine Rose.
Fashion.summary:
Leadership change dominates luxury and high fashion today. WWD reports that Justin Boxford is preparing to succeed John Idol as chief executive of Capri Holdings, the parent of Michael Kors and Jimmy Choo, though no official announcement has been made. The report comes as would-be buyers reportedly circle the group after the failed Tapestry deal.

Creative leadership is also moving. Martine Rose has been appointed creative director of Balenciaga, succeeding Pierpaolo Piccioli, while Tod's has lost Matteo Tamburini. Meanwhile, eBay data suggest new creative directors are lifting resale demand, with searches for Matthieu Blazy up 291% after his first Chanel collection.

Business results were mostly firm. On grew sales 17.2% in the third quarter, with Asia-Pacific up 31.9%, and Safilo returned to North American growth. Rhode, bought by E.l.f. Beauty, is on pace to be the fastest beauty brand to reach $1 billion in sales.
